# Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) Summary
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a class of generative models formulated as a zero-sum game between two neural networks: a generator and a discriminator. The generator learns to produce data samples (e.g., images) that imitate a reference distribution, while the discriminator aims to distinguish between real samples from the reference data and those produced by the generator. The training process involves alternating updates of both networks using backpropagation, with the generator trying to "fool" the discriminator and the discriminator striving to correctly identify generated versus real samples. Mathematically, the classic GAN objective leads the generator to match its output distribution to the real data, while the discriminator converges to a function measuring the likelihood ratio between real and generated data (Jensen–Shannon divergence). GANs are implicit generative models, standing out for their ability to efficiently generate high-quality samples in a single pass.
Numerous variants of GANs have emerged, including conditional GANs (which generate samples conditioned on additional inputs), Wasserstein GANs (using the Wasserstein distance for better training stability), CycleGANs (for unpaired image-to-image translation), and hybrid models like VAEGAN. Alternative architectures use convolutional, self-attention, or transformer-based neural networks. Despite their power, GANs suffer from training instabilities such as mode collapse and vanishing gradients, which are mitigated by techniques like curriculum learning, two time-scale update rule, and data augmentation. GANs have wide-ranging applications in scientific modeling, medical imaging, art creation, fashion, adversarial media generation (deepfakes), and more. They have enabled notable advancements in high-fidelity data synthesis, domain translation, and creative AI.
